Dear Ujjwal,
You said on the phone that current electricity makes no sense. It didn't for me either, until Sunday. So here's what worked for me, before Thursday's test.
I was staring at the circuit diagrams and then I looked out at the water tank on our roof. And I thought: what if the wire is a pipe and the current is water flowing through it?
Then the rest fell into place. Voltage is like the pressure, how hard the water is pushed from the tank. Resistance is a narrow bit of pipe that slows the flow. So if you add more narrow bits one after another, less water gets through. That's why bulbs in a row get dimmer!
I solved six questions from the exercise after that, and I got five right.
Try it with the tank picture and tell me if it works for you too.
Noor

Zeenat, you asked on the bus why Raghav suddenly started getting circuit questions right. So, here's what happened.
Last week, our physics sir asked why two bulbs in series glow less than one. I had no idea. At home I was watering Ammi's plants with the hose, and I pinched the hose by mistake. The water just dribbled out.
And I was like, wait. That's resistance. The pinch is the resistor. The tap pressure is the voltage. The water flowing is the current.
So two bulbs in series, that's two pinches on the same hose. Less water. Less current. Dimmer bulbs.
Then I tried parallel. Two hoses from the same tap. Each gets its own flow. Brighter.
Honestly I felt kind of stupid it took a hose to explain it. But now I don't have to memorise, I can just picture it.

I'm Shalini, and last May our room at the top of the building was like an oven. We couldn't afford a cooler, and the ones in the shop were big metal boxes with pumps.
My friend Nilesh said, "Just watch a video and copy one."
But I didn't want to copy a box. I wanted to understand. So I asked myself: when I come out of a swimming pool, why do I feel cold even in summer? Because the water on my skin is drying, and drying pulls heat away.
So all I needed was water drying where the air was moving. I hung a wet cotton dupatta across the window, where the evening breeze came in, and put a bucket below so it could drip.
The room dropped from unbearable to okay. Not a miracle. But I understood why it worked, and I could fix it when it dried out.

I'm Dolma, and in my first year at the logistics company, the nightly delivery report took six hours. Everyone accepted it. My senior Jomon told me, "It's always been like that. Don't touch it."
But it was low risk to look. I wasn't changing anything, just reading. So I asked the simplest question: what has to happen between the raw delivery records and the final report? Only three things, really. Read the records, add them up by region, write the result.
Then I traced what the job actually did. It read the records. Then it copied everything into a temporary table. Then it copied that temporary table into another temporary table with the same columns. Then it added up.
That middle copy did nothing. It was left over from some old migration.
I showed Jomon. We removed it in a test on a Sunday. Six hours became one hour fifty. Jomon just said, "Huh." I think that was a compliment.

The board exams were eight weeks away, and Anjali's younger brother had just started drum classes in the room next to hers. Evenings would be noisy from now on.
She sat on her bed with a notebook and flipped the question around. Not "how do I do well?" but "how would I definitely do badly?"
She wrote fast. Stay up all night before each paper. Sleep five hours. Never touch past papers. Study only on the loud evenings. Keep the phone next to the book.
Her friend Rafiq called. "What are you doing?"
"Making a list of how to fail."
"Very motivating."
"No, listen. Now I just do the opposite." She turned the page. Sleep by eleven. Study the hard subjects in the quiet early mornings. One past paper every Sunday. Phone in the kitchen.
Rafiq was quiet. "Can you send me that list?"

qa.a: Phone in the kitchen.

qa.q: What else could Anjali add to make the list work, and why?

In the Andheri coaching centre's library, Arohi was staring at a blank timetable. Her friend Madhav leaned over. "Still empty?"
"I don't know where to start."
"Then start from the other end. What would guarantee you mess up the boards?"
Arohi thought, then wrote. All-nighters before exams. Skipping breakfast. No practice papers. Starting maths only in February. Studying in bed.
She looked at the list for a minute. "Okay. That's weirdly easy."
Then she wrote the opposite beside each one. Sleep seven hours, no all-nighters. Breakfast before the first session. One past paper every Saturday. Maths from this week. Study at the table only.
She stuck it in her folder. "This I can actually follow."
Madhav grinned. "Now I'm making one."

qa.q: What did Arohi write as the opposite of no practice papers?
qa.a: One past paper every Saturday.

qa.q: How did Arohi feel after listing the ways to mess up?
qa.a: She felt surprised and more confident, calling it weirdly easy and saying she could actually follow the new plan.

qa.q: Which other approach could Arohi add to the inversion list?
qa.a: She could set a small weekly goal, like a mock score to reach, so the plan also moves her toward something.

qa.q: How might Madhav be affected by watching Arohi make the list?
qa.a: Madhav is inspired enough to make his own, seeing how quickly the blank timetable became something useful.

grounding: It shows a student asking what would guarantee failure in exams, listing cramming, skipped sleep and no past papers, and building a routine that avoids each.
